meta.name: Why Dogs Eat Poop (Coprophagia) and How to Stop It
meta.tagline: It is gross, it is common, and it is often manageable with a calm plan.
meta.excerpt: Dogs eat poop for normal and medical reasons. Here is how to rule out health causes and manage it with cleanup, leash skills, and a solid leave it.
meta.meta_description: Why do dogs eat poop? Learn the common causes, when to call the vet, and force-free ways to manage it with cleanup, leash skills, and leave it.

intro.label: Why It Happens
intro.heading: Why Your Dog Eats Poop (and Why You Are Not Alone)
intro.html:
You step outside for a quick potty break, look away for a second, and your dog is already investigating something they absolutely should not. Then comes the kisses. If this is your life right now, take a breath. Eating feces, known as coprophagia, is one of the most common things dog owners ask about, and it does not mean you did something wrong.

Veterinary and training sources describe stool eating as a fairly common behavior, especially in puppies, even though it is unpleasant for us. In many dogs it looks like a habit or a scavenging instinct. In some dogs it can point to a health or care issue that deserves a vet visit. Some puppies lose interest as they mature, but research suggests many dogs keep the habit, so it helps to have a plan. The smart approach has two tracks: check for medical causes, and manage and train the behavior at the same time.

This guide covers the most common reasons dogs do this, what a vet may want to rule out, how to keep your family healthy, and the practical steps that often help: fast cleanup, better leash skills, a reliable “leave it,” and simple routine changes. No fix works overnight for every dog, but many owners can make real progress with consistency.

Quick answer: Rule out medical causes with your vet, remove access to stool as quickly as you can, teach a force-free “leave it,” meet your dog’s exercise, food, and attention needs, and wash your hands after cleanup. Never punish. Punishment may make dogs sneakier rather than less interested.

care.label: What To Do
care.heading: How to Understand and Manage Stool Eating
care.html:
Common reasons dogs eat feces

There is rarely one single cause, and in many dogs experts cannot point to just one. These are the reasons most often discussed by veterinarians and veterinary behaviorists. Some are better supported than others:

  • Normal puppy exploring. Puppies investigate the world with their mouths. Some try stool and lose interest as they mature, but others keep the habit, especially if it is rewarded or repeated.
  • Learned habit. If a dog finds it rewarding, or gets a big reaction from you, the behavior can stick.
  • Scavenging instinct. Dogs are natural opportunists. Cat litter, goose droppings, and horse manure can smell like a snack to some dogs.
  • Boredom, stress, or lack of exercise. These are sometimes suggested as causes, but they are not proven. Dogs left alone for long stretches or confined in small spaces may pick up the habit, though research has not clearly confirmed this.
  • Past punishment for accidents. It is commonly reported that dogs punished for house-training accidents may eat stool to hide the evidence, but this explanation is unproven.
  • Diet or appetite changes. A dog that is always hungry or is not absorbing nutrients well may be more tempted.
  • Medical issues. Parasites, digestive or absorption problems, and certain conditions or medications that increase appetite can play a role. Only a vet can sort this out.
SituationPossibilitiesBest first step
Young puppy, new habitMay be normal exploringQuick cleanup, supervision, mention at next vet visit
Adult dog, sudden new habitCould possibly be a medical or stress trigger, among other thingsCall your vet for a check-up
Eats other animals’ stool on walksMay be a scavenging habitLeash skills and leave it training
Eats own stool, with weight loss or loose stoolCould be a health issue; only a vet can say whichVet visit with a stool sample

This table is only a rough guide. It cannot tell you what is going on with your dog.

Step 1: Talk to your vet first

Before you launch a training plan, book a vet visit, especially if the behavior is new, intense, or paired with other changes. Your vet may check for intestinal parasites, review your dog’s diet and feeding amounts, and look for signs of digestive or hormonal problems. Bring a fresh stool sample if your vet asks for one, and write down when the behavior started, what stool your dog goes for, and anything else that has changed.

Only a vet can diagnose conditions such as pancreatic or malabsorption problems, so please do not try to work out the cause from symptoms or the table above. Do not change medications on your own. If your dog takes any medication, ask your vet whether it could affect appetite or digestion.

Step 2: Remove the opportunity

Management is often helpful, because every time your dog successfully eats stool, it may reinforce the habit. Think of it as preventing practice while you build better skills.

  • Pick up your dog’s stool right away, every time. Go out with your dog on a leash, even in a fenced yard, so you can clean up before they reach it.
  • Keep litter boxes out of reach, such as in a closed room, on a high shelf, or in a covered or enclosed box your dog cannot get into. Small dogs can squeeze through or jump over many gates.
  • Scoop the yard daily, and check for droppings from wildlife or neighborhood pets.
  • Keep potty trips boring and short. Go out, let your dog do their business, then reward them with a treat or praise and head back in.
  • Supervise puppies closely, and use a crate or pen when you cannot watch them. Our crate training guide can help you set that up calmly.

Step 3: Build better leash skills

Many dogs grab stool on walks, and a few simple leash habits can help:

  • Use a standard leash of a comfortable length rather than a long, loose one, so you can steer around trouble spots.
  • Scan ahead. If you spot droppings, calmly change direction before your dog reaches them.
  • Reward your dog for looking at you. Treat each time they check in with you on a walk, especially near tempting areas.
  • Use a well-fitted harness or flat collar. Avoid prong, choke, or shock tools. They can create fear and stress, and they do not teach your dog what to do instead.
  • Carry small, high-value treats so you always have something better than stool to offer.
    One option: Blue Buffalo Bits Soft Training Treats, Beef (19 oz) on Amazon. Soft, bite-size training treats with real beef as the first ingredient, small enough for rapid repetitions. Keep treats to about 10% of daily calories.

Step 4: Teach a solid “leave it”

A reliable “leave it” is often a helpful training tool for this problem. Practice in a quiet room first, with ordinary treats, long before you expect it to work around real poop.

  1. Hold a low-value treat in a closed fist. Let your dog sniff, lick, or paw at it. Stay quiet and wait.
  2. The moment your dog pulls away or looks at you, say “yes” and give a better treat from your other hand.
  3. Repeat until your dog turns away from the fist right away. Then add the cue “leave it” just before presenting the fist.
  4. Move to a treat on the floor under your hand, then uncovered on the floor, rewarding every time your dog chooses to look at you.
  5. Practice with more tempting items, then on walks with something mildly interesting like a dropped leaf.
  6. Use “leave it” near real stool only after your dog is succeeding in many other places, and keep a leash on for safety. Reward heavily with a very special treat.

Also teach a happy “come” or “let’s go” cue. Calling your dog away from stool and rewarding them for coming often works better than trying to take something out of their mouth.

Step 5: Meet daily needs

Some experts suggest that dogs with plenty of exercise, mental work, and companionship may be less likely to turn to odd habits, though this is not proven. These things are good for your dog either way. Add sniff walks, food puzzles, chew toys that are safe for your dog, and short training games. Make sure your dog is eating a complete and balanced food, which means one that meets AAFCO nutritional standards for their life stage. Ask your vet if your dog’s food type, portion size, or meal schedule needs adjusting.

If you have a young puppy who is also mouthy in general, our guide on stopping puppy biting and mouthing covers many of the same ideas around redirecting that busy mouth.

Keep your family healthy

Dogs that eat stool can pick up intestinal parasites and germs, and some of these, such as roundworms and Giardia, can pass to people. Face licking is one way that can happen, so homes with children, older adults, or anyone with a weakened immune system should take extra care. Wash hands with soap and water after picking up stool or getting licked, and help young children do the same. Discourage licking around faces and mouths. Ask your vet how often to do fecal testing and what parasite prevention suits your dog.

What about deterrent products?

You will see many food additives and chews marketed to make stool taste bad. Veterinary sources generally note that evidence for these is limited and results vary from dog to dog. If you want to try this kind of product, ask your vet first so you can pick something safe and avoid anything that could upset your dog’s stomach or interact with medications. Treat any product as a helper, not a replacement for cleanup and training.

special.label: Avoid & Escalate
special.heading: Mistakes to Avoid and When to Get Help
special.html:
Common mistakes

  • Punishing or scolding. Yelling, rubbing a dog’s nose in stool, or physical corrections can increase anxiety and may teach dogs to eat stool faster or hide it. Veterinary behaviorists recommend force-free methods instead.
  • Making a big scene. A dramatic reaction can turn stool into an exciting game of chase. Stay calm, call your dog, and reward them for coming to you.
  • Leaving stool lying around. Even a great training plan struggles if the temptation is always available.
  • Adding unsafe seasonings or home remedies. Do not put hot sauce, pepper, or random supplements on stool or in food without asking your vet. Some can irritate your dog’s mouth or stomach.
  • Skipping the vet visit. Training can mask a medical problem for a while, but it will not fix it.
  • Expecting instant results. Habits built over months take weeks of consistent practice to change, and some dogs never fully stop. Everyone in the household needs to follow the same plan.

When to call your vet

Call your vet promptly if stool eating comes with any of the following. Your vet is the one who can work out what is behind them:

  • Weight loss, a poor coat, or a big change in appetite or thirst
  • Loose, greasy, bloody, or unusually frequent stools
  • Vomiting, low energy, or belly discomfort
  • A sudden start in an adult dog that never did this before
  • Eating stool from animals that may have been sick or treated with medication

Emergency note: Stool from animals taking certain medications can be harmful to dogs that eat it. If your dog may have eaten stool containing medication, or eaten something toxic along with it, contact your veterinarian or an animal poison control center right away. The ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center and Pet Poison Helpline are two options, and fees may apply. Have your dog’s weight, what they ate, and when ready.

When to bring in a trainer or behaviorist

If your vet finds no medical cause and the habit continues despite a few weeks of consistent management and training, consider a certified force-free trainer. Look for someone who uses reward-based methods and will not recommend prong, shock, or “alpha” techniques. If your dog also shows signs of anxiety, such as pacing, destructive behavior when alone, or panting and drooling, ask your vet about a referral to a veterinary behaviorist.

Your quick decision checklist

  1. Has the vet checked for medical causes, including a stool sample? If not, schedule that first.
  2. Is your dog supervised on a leash during every potty trip?
  3. Is stool picked up immediately, indoors and out?
  4. Are litter boxes and wildlife droppings out of reach?
  5. Is “leave it” practiced daily with rewards that beat stool?
  6. Does your dog get enough exercise, sniffing time, and mental work?
  7. Is everyone washing hands after cleanup and face licks?
  8. Is the whole household using the same calm, no-punishment approach?
  9. If progress stalls after several weeks, have you asked a vet, trainer, or behaviorist for help?

If you are newer to dog ownership, you may also like our guide for first-time owners, which covers the everyday basics that make habits like this easier to manage.

faq.q: Is it normal for dogs to eat poop?
faq.a: It is common, and veterinary and training sources describe it as a fairly frequent behavior, especially in puppies. Often it looks like a habit or scavenging instinct rather than a serious problem. Still, mention it to your vet, since parasites, diet, or health issues can sometimes contribute.

faq.q: Will my puppy grow out of eating poop?
faq.a: Some puppies lose interest as they mature, especially if owners clean up quickly and avoid giving the habit extra attention. But research suggests many dogs continue, so it may fade without being guaranteed to. If it continues past puppyhood or gets worse, check in with your vet and add leave it practice.

faq.q: Can eating poop make my dog sick?
faq.a: It can. Stool may carry intestinal parasites and germs, especially from other animals, and some stool may contain medication residue. Some of these parasites can also pass to people. Many dogs seem fine afterward, but if yours has vomiting, diarrhea, or low energy, contact your vet. Quick cleanup and handwashing matter.

faq.q: Do food additives or deterrent chews stop dogs from eating poop?
faq.a: Results vary, and veterinary sources generally say evidence for these products is limited. Some owners see improvement and many do not. Ask your vet before trying one, and treat it as a small helper alongside cleanup, leash skills, and training instead of a stand-alone fix.

faq.q: Should I punish my dog for eating poop?
faq.a: No. Punishment, scolding, or rubbing a dog's nose in stool can create fear and anxiety, and dogs may start eating stool faster or hiding it. Veterinary behaviorists recommend a calm, force-free approach: prevent access, call your dog away, and reward good choices.

faq.q: Why does my dog eat cat poop?
faq.a: Many dogs find cat feces tasty, partly because of the smell and the food it can contain. It is a common scavenging habit. Keep litter boxes where your dog cannot reach them, such as in a closed room, on a high shelf, or in a covered or enclosed box. Gates and cat-sized openings may not stop small dogs. Teach a strong leave it too.

faq.q: When should I see a vet about stool eating?
faq.a: See your vet if the habit is new in an adult dog, or comes with weight loss, changes in appetite or stool, vomiting, or low energy. It is also smart to mention it at routine visits. Your vet can check for parasites and review your dog's diet and health.
